headline: Bhutan Becomes Second Country to Eliminate Dog-Transmitted Rabies
meta_description: Bhutan officially recognized by WHO for eliminating dog-transmitted human rabies, joining Mexico as only the second country globally to achieve this milestone.
summary_short: Bhutan has officially eliminated dog-transmitted rabies as a public health threat, becoming only the second country worldwide to achieve this milestone ahead of World Ra…
body:
The World Health Organization has officially recognized Bhutan for eliminating dog-transmitted human rabies, making it the second country globally to achieve this landmark public health victory—and the first in Southeast Asia. With zero human deaths from dog-mediated rabies recorded since June 2023, Bhutan has demonstrated the resources and systems necessary to prevent the disease's return. The achievement arrives in time for World Rabies Day on September 28, marking a triumph for a nation that has long pursued interconnected approaches to protecting human, animal, and environmental health. Nearly 99% of all human rabies cases worldwide stem from infected dog bites or scratches, and once symptoms appear, the disease is almost always fatal—making Bhutan's success particularly meaningful.

The country's breakthrough came through persistence and coordination across government ministries. A 2021 Royal Decree launched the Nationwide Accelerated Dog Population Management and Rabies Control Programme, jointly implemented by Bhutan's Ministry of Health and Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock. Field health teams and veterinarians, supported by civilian volunteers, achieved 100% sterilization of the free-roaming dog population while vaccinating more than 90% of such dogs against rabies—exceeding the WHO's recommended 70% threshold needed to break transmission chains. Equally important, post-exposure prophylaxis treatment, which prevents rabies infection after exposure, remains universally free across all 20 of Bhutan's districts through the Bhutan Health Trust Fund.

Bhutan's success reflects what the WHO calls a "One Health" approach, recognizing that animal, human, and environmental wellbeing are inseparable. The World Organization for Animal Health stressed that validation is a milestone, not a finish line—sustained vigilance, vaccination coverage, wildlife surveillance, and cross-border collaboration remain essential. Just days later, Chile became the first South American country to receive the same recognition, suggesting momentum is building toward the global goal of eliminating human rabies deaths by 2030.
quick_facts: Bhutan: second country globally to eliminate dog-transmitted rabies
Zero human deaths from dog rabies since June 2023
100% sterilization of free-roaming dogs achieved nationwide
Over 90% of dogs vaccinated against rabies across country
Post-exposure treatment free in all 20 districts
